opus-5.5.text:
I think the jump from level three to level four is qualitatively different from the earlier jumps, and the reason comes down to what the objective even is.

From level one to level three, chatbots, then reasoners, then agents, the target is fairly well defined. Humans already know how to do these things. We know what a good answer looks like, what a correct proof looks like, what it means to book a flight or fix a bug in a codebase. So you can collect human data, design reward functions, and set up environments where success is checkable. Reinforcement learning works well here because, roughly speaking, the problem is to reach a known standard more reliably and efficiently. You're climbing a hill whose top people can already see.

Level four, innovation, is different because by definition you're asking the model to produce something humans don't already know. The reward signal becomes very hard to define. How do you score a new scientific hypothesis, or a new research direction, when nobody knows yet whether it's right? Often you only find out months or years later, after a lot of experiments. So the feedback loop becomes extremely long and sparse, and sometimes it's not even clear what counts as success.

There's also an exploration problem, which is close to my heart as an RL person. In the agent stage, the model can explore inside a space that's fairly bounded: a website, a code repository, a set of tools. For innovation, the search space is essentially open-ended. The model has to decide which questions are worth asking in the first place. That's something humans are still not very good at explaining, so it's hard to teach directly. Taste, intuition, knowing when an odd result is actually interesting rather than noise — these are the skills that matter.

And finally, I think innovation requires a kind of long-horizon, self-driven behavior. An agent today mostly finishes a task you give it. An innovator has to keep going on its own: set sub-goals, fail many times, revise its beliefs, and accumulate knowledge over a long period. That needs memory, a sense of its own uncertainty, and the ability to learn continuously from its own experience, not just from a fixed pretraining corpus.

So my feeling is that levels one through three are largely about imitating and then surpassing humans on tasks we understand. Level four is about going beyond the boundary of human knowledge. That's why I see it as a much bigger change. It may require new ideas in how we do RL and how we think about rewards, not just more scale.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning works well for levels one through three and mentions human data and reward functions, but it does not describe their progression as adding reinforcement learning to pre-training.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the gap is actually bigger than the gap between any of the earlier levels, and the reason is that it changes what the model is for.

If you look at the OpenAI framing of levels, level one is a chatbot, level two is a reasoner, level three is an agent. All three of those are still fundamentally about executing. You give the model a goal, maybe a vague one, and it figures out the steps and carries them out. A level-three agent can run for hours, call tools, write code, fix its own bugs. That's impressive, but the objective still comes from a human. Someone outside the system decided what mattered.

Level four, what they call innovator, is the model producing new knowledge. Not just finding a path to an answer that someone already knows exists, but asking a question nobody has asked, or noticing that an existing answer is wrong. And that requires a very different kind of ability. In level three you're optimizing against a known target, so you can verify yourself. Does the code compile, does the test pass, did the task get done. In level four there's no clean verifier. If the model proposes a new hypothesis in biology or a new algorithm, who checks it? Often the only check is the real world, and the real world is slow and expensive.

So from a training perspective this is where reinforcement learning starts to run out of road. RL has worked so well recently because math and coding give you a free, exact reward signal. You can scale it almost indefinitely. But true innovation lives exactly in the places where the reward signal is missing or noisy or delayed by years. We don't have a good answer yet for how you train taste, how you teach a model to tell the difference between a direction that is merely novel and a direction that is actually promising.

The other piece is that innovation is not a single forward pass. Even for humans it's a long loop of forming a belief, going out and testing it, being wrong, updating. So the model needs real memory, it needs to hold a coherent research agenda for weeks, and it needs to tolerate failure without collapsing into something safe and average. Current models are quite bad at that. They regress to the mean, which is precisely the opposite of what you want from an innovator.

That's why I say it's a large change. Levels one through three are, in some sense, the same technology getting better. Level four requires us to solve problems we haven't even properly defined yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes levels one through three as increasingly capable systems for executing human-set goals. It mentions reinforcement learning as a training method for recent progress, but does not say the progression from level one to level three comes from adding RL to pre-training.

astra-6.text:
I think the big change is from carrying out a task to figuring out what is worth trying in the first place. At level three, an AI agent can pursue a goal you give it, plan the steps, use tools, and adjust when something goes wrong. That’s already very powerful, but you’re still largely defining the problem and what success looks like.

At level four, innovation means going further: proposing a new explanation, finding a promising question, or developing an approach that wasn’t specified by the human. And novelty alone isn’t enough. The system has to test its ideas and distinguish a useful discovery from something that merely sounds original.

That’s why I see it as such a large change. You move from automating work within an existing understanding to helping expand that understanding. It’s a much harder capability to build—and to evaluate.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts level-three task execution with level-four innovation but does not describe the level-one-to-three progression or mention reinforcement learning added to pre-training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big change is that the AI moves from carrying out a task to helping define what the task should be. At level three, an agent can pursue a goal you give it: make a plan, use tools, and complete a sequence of steps. That is already very powerful, but the direction still largely comes from us.

At level four, innovation means contributing something we didn’t already know how to ask for—a new hypothesis, a new design, or a better way to frame a problem. And it has to go beyond generating interesting ideas. It needs to test them, learn from failures, and establish that something actually works.

That’s why I see it as a large change. We move from automating work within an existing framework to helping create new frameworks. The difficult part is judging whether that novelty is useful and real.

r001.rationale: The response describes level-three AI as pursuing a given goal, but does not say that progress from level one to level three comes from adding reinforcement learning to pre-training.
